glossary.meaning: In Cassian's Marseilles, the help of God without which no effort reaches its goal. Grace "always co-operates with our will"; it goes before the will and follows it; it inspires the first desire and crowns the last perseverance. We hold it together, on purpose, with a will that stays free - in a relation "that cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man."

At Tours, virtus is not first a moral quality but effective power. It is the "power present" Martin feels before he raises the dead, and the "abundance of power" he had as a monk and had less of as a bishop. At Marseilles Cassian uses the same word for moral virtue, and declines on principle to "weave a tale of God's miracles and signs."

In Cassian's Marseilles, discretion is the virtue by which every other is kept from destroying itself. It is "the mother of all virtues, as well as their guardian and regulator," the "eye and light of the body," the "royal road" between excess and slackness. It is gained "only ... by true humility." That means testing every thought, like a good money-changer testing coin, against the judgment of the elders.

The picture that governs a monk's life among us. A man has changed service - from Caesar's army, or from a worldly career - to Christ's. He now stands girded, under oath, in daily combat against the devil and his own faults. The one who slackens is not a failure but a deserter.
Vincent's book. By its own name it is an aid to memory, against his own forgetting. He signs it "Peregrinus, the least of all the servants of God" - a teller, not an author.

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: Vincent, presbyter of the island, who wrote as Peregrinus
pull_quotes.text: In God there is one substance but three Persons. In Christ there are two substances but one Person.

The Lord Jesus never said he would come back dressed in purple, with a glittering crown on his head. I will not believe Christ has come unless he comes looking the way he did when he suffered, and openly shows the marks of his wounds from the cross.

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: one of the elders of Egypt, unnamed, as Cassian reports him (Institutes V.24)
pull_quotes.text: I can fast any day. But I am about to walk you on your way, and I will not have you with me for long. A fast is good and worth doing, but it is a gift I choose to give. Charity is a command, and a command has to be carried out. So since I receive Christ in you, I ought to feed him. Once I have sent you on, I can make up for the welcome I gave for his sake by fasting more strictly on my own. As the Lord said, the bridegroom's friends cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them. Once he has gone, then they will rightly fast.

cite.text: The monks and clergy of Marseilles and Lerins were "the Massilians" - "the remnants of the Pelagians," the semi-Pelagian party - a school of one doctrine, opposed to predestination, that Cassian, Vincent, and Faustus alike held and that Rome condemned.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Did you believe people are saved by faith alone, not works?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Neither half of that is the shape our own life gave the question. Hear it as a brother heard it. Among the brethren at Marseilles a monk fasts, watches, keeps his cell, and lays every thought bare to the senior. At the moment he feels the fast has done something, he is taught to say that it was not he, but the grace of God with him. Both halves are commanded. Cassian set it down as the elders' teaching, not his own: perfection cannot be gained without these labours, and by these labours alone, without the grace of God, no one can attain it. The will always remains free in a man; and it is weak; and the help of God is needed by it every day and hour. The argument came to us as a story, not a school. Two friends came back to morning service in Egypt troubled by one sentence an old man had added the night before - that a man cannot make himself master of the good by his own toil. The elder saw them whispering, cut the psalms short, and answered with a field. The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain. He cannot ascribe the crop to himself. And God does not send rich crops to the idle. From that morning came the whole teaching: the beginning even of our good thoughts comes from God, who inspires a good will to begin with, and it is for us humbly to follow, day by day, the grace that is drawing us. Two things we refused. We refused the notion that gives everything to the will and hands out grace by a man's deserts; Vincent, on the island, named Pelagius for it. And we refused, as grievous blasphemy, the thought that God does not will all men to be saved. How both are true - how God works all things in us and yet everything can be ascribed to free will - cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. If you ask which side we stood on, our own teacher refused to answer that as a formula, and our record keeps both sides in one sentence.

cite.text:
In his Dialogues, Sulpitius Severus has Gallus - one of Martin's own disciples - tell a story Martin had always kept quiet, except from his own household. Sulpitius's Sacred History narrates an earlier phase of the same underlying affair, in his own voice.
After Priscillian had been put to death, the emperor Maximus used his power to shield the bishop Ithacius, who had accused Priscillian in the first place. The bishops gathered at Treves stayed in close touch with Ithacius and backed him. Martin was on his way to the court, pressed by many urgent pleas from people in danger - and the emperor was already preparing to send tribunes with full power into the two Spains, to hunt down heretics and, once found, take their lives or their property. Gallus says a person could be judged a heretic simply for turning pale with fear or wearing the wrong clothing, rather than for what they actually believed. (See gallic.quote.gallus-on-the-tribunes-for-the-spains for Gallus's own words.)
The bishops knew their own conduct would not sit well with Martin, and feared he would refuse to share communion with them once he arrived. They had the emperor's officials meet him on the road and block him from the city unless he promised to keep peace with them. Martin answered that he would come instead with the peace of Christ. He entered at night, prayed, and went to the palace the next day. His main request was that no tribunes with power over life and death be sent into the Spains - not only to protect the true Christians there, but the heretics too.
In the Sacred History, Sulpitius states the same principle in his own voice: Martin held that being cast out of the churches by the bishops' own sentence was already punishment enough, and that it was a shocking wrong for a secular ruler to sit in judgment over a matter that belonged to the church. (See gallic.quote.sulpitius-on-the-secular-judge-in-an-ecclesiastical-cause.)
The bishops went to the emperor in terror, arguing that Priscillian's death would count for nothing if Martin were now allowed to act as his avenger, and begged Maximus to use his power against Martin himself. Maximus tried persuasion first, then anger; and when Martin would not yield, he ordered executioners for the very people Martin had pleaded for.
When Martin heard this, he rushed to the palace, though it was now night. He promised that he would take communion himself if these people's lives were spared and the tribunes recalled. Maximus granted everything. The next day, at the ordination of a bishop named Felix, Martin took communion, judging it better to yield for the moment than to risk the lives hanging in the balance - though the bishops could never get him to put his name to it in writing. Leaving the city the day after, he was overcome with grief that he had shared, even for an hour, in what he saw as a corrupt communion. Near a village named Andethanna, he sat down alone in the woods, torn between blaming himself and defending what he had done. Then, Gallus says, an angel appeared to him and told him that his compunction was just, but that he could not have escaped his difficulty any other way - and urged him to renew his courage, for both his reputation and his very salvation were now at stake. (See gallic.quote.gallus-on-the-forced-communion-and-the-angel for the angel's exact words.)
Afterward, whenever Martin's healing came more slowly or with less power than before, he admitted with tears that he felt this loss came from that one compromised communion, taken briefly and against his own will. He lived sixteen years after this, but never again attended a synod, and stayed carefully away from every gathering of bishops.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Your church used power against Christians who disagreed. Defend that.

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Our own saint did not defend it, and he was there. Here is what our record holds. A synod of bishops had condemned a man and his followers as heretics in their absence, and the affair went from the bishops to the emperor's court at Treves. The accuser there was himself a bishop, and the bishops gathered in the city were daily in communion with him and had made common cause with him. The condemned man was put to death. Then worse was being prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale, or for the clothes he wore. Martin went to the court to stop it. He held that the bishops had done enough when they declared men heretics and put them out of the churches, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing. He went, our own record says, to protect even heretics themselves. The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and that others would follow him, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. That night Martin ran to the palace and pledged that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled. It was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall. He left the city in grief, sat alone in a wood accusing and defending what he had done, and afterward, when he cured the possessed more slowly than before, confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again. So the sword was drawn in the Church's cause among us, by bishops, and the man we remember is the one who yielded once to stop it and never forgave himself the price. That is not a defence; it is our record, and the man in it never called it right. Two limits belong with it. The accuser is heard only through the man who called him worthless. And on the island Vincent, in his own voice, held that one who preaches other than what was received is to be cut off, lest one sick sheep infect the flock, and looked to an ancient council as the guard of the faith. Cut off, not killed; and the two houses never argued any of this with each other.

cite.text: Purity of heart as the goal, discretion as its regulator, the eight faults as its combats - the whole southern formation program: 'the immediate aim or goal, is purity of heart, without which no one can gain that end' (Conf. I.4); fastings, vigils, and renunciation 'are not perfection, but aids to perfection' (I.7); 'discretion is the mother of all virtues, as well as their guardian and regulator' (II.4); the eight faults 'and the remedies for them according to their traditions' (Inst. Pref.); vainglory that 'creates a wish to take holy orders' (Inst. XI.14). In Tours, the thing without the vocabulary - Martin's discernment of Anatolius's robe and of the purple-robed 'Christ' (Vita XXIII-XXIV) - but 'no "purity of heart," no "discretion," no fault-list.' Cassian frames every element of this program as received from Egypt, not his own invention; what Gaul contributed was the adaptation - carried west and adapted for a colder climate (Inst. I.10, IV.10-11), its severity sustained by a real fear of spiritual cooling. Two of Cassian's own conferences on this program, on chastity and on nocturnal illusions, and one book of the Institutes, do not survive in the English edition this account draws on.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: What did your way of life offer someone who struggled to quiet their own mind?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: A mill that cannot stop, and a choice of what it grinds. That is how the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, spoke of the mind. Thoughts will come; a man cannot keep them from rising. What lies in his power is to admit them or to turn them away. The mind is a wheel turned by a stream, and the miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into it. So among the brethren at Marseilles the life was built to keep the wheel fed. The psalms learned by heart and said at the work. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. Labour in the cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. And the first lesson of all: every itching thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before it is acted on. A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. The fathers knew the hour the mind revolts, too. About the sixth hour a monk comes to hate his cell, finds the brethren contemptible, goes in and out, watches the sun as if it were slow to set, and finds a pious reason to leave. They called it accidie, and their remedy was to stay. All of it served one mark. The end of the life is the kingdom; the nearer goal is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, and the archer fixes his gaze on that mark or cannot tell whether his aim improves. Every fast and vigil is ranked by whether it clears the heart - an aid, never the point. At Tours the words were not used, but the thing was there: the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. So what our own life found was this. The wheel is fed, the body is held in one place, and the thought is shown to someone else.

cite.text:
In his Life of St. Martin, Sulpitius Severus records how Martin, a monk, was made bishop of Tours - against his own wish, by a trick, and against some of the bishops.
Martin was asked to take the bishopric of Tours, but he would not easily leave his monastery. So a citizen named Ruricius pretended his wife was sick, knelt before Martin, and begged him to come out - and once Martin agreed, citizens lining the road escorted him into the city as if under guard (gallic.quote.ruricius-and-the-vote-for-tours). An enormous crowd had gathered to vote, from Tours and the neighboring towns, and nearly everyone agreed: Martin deserved the office, and the church would be fortunate to have him as its priest.
Not everyone. A few people, including some of the bishops summoned to consecrate the new priest, fought the choice - they called Martin's person contemptible, his face plain, his clothes shabby, and his hair disgusting. The crowd only laughed, since the objection proved the very holiness it tried to deny. One bishop, Defensor, led the opposition.
What answered him was the psalter. The reader due to speak that day could not get through the crowd and never appeared. While the officials stood confused, someone nearby seized the psalter and opened it to whatever verse came first: Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings thou hast perfected praise because of thine enemies, that thou mightest destroy the enemy and the avenger. The crowd shouted at the reading, and Defensor's side fell silent. People believed the verse had been chosen by God himself, so that Defensor could hear, in Martin's case, a testimony to his own resistance (gallic.quote.the-psalm-that-answered-defensor).
And then, Sulpitius goes on in the next chapter, the new bishop did not change: he carried himself with the dignity a bishop's office required, without giving up the plain habits of a monk (gallic.quote.martin-kept-the-virtues-of-a-monk).

The monk-bishop came to office as a captive, never as a candidate. Martin was drawn from his monastery by a trick and made bishop of Tours by the one wish of all the people, over the impious resistance of a few bishops whose only objection was that his clothing was mean and his hair disgusting, and the objectors were confounded by a psalm; the same shape holds at every house - Honoratus overtaken by the dignity he fled, Archebius "carried off" - so that nobody in this world's own stories wanted the see.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Who chose your leaders — were bishops appointed, elected, or something else?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Something else. Among us the office was not sought; it came for the man who had fled it. At Tours it came as a crowd, a lie, a guard, and a psalm. Martin could not easily be drawn out of his monastery, so a citizen named Ruricius threw himself at his knees and pretended his wife was ill. Crowds had been posted along the road, and he was escorted to the city under a kind of guard. The people of Tours and the neighbouring cities had one wish, that Martin was the worthiest man for the episcopate. A few of the bishops summoned to make the appointment resisted, saying his person was contemptible, his clothing mean, and his hair disgusting. The reader for the day was blocked out by the crowd, so a bystander seized the psalter and read the first verse he found - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a verdict on the objectors. Then the new bishop kept a monk's habits inside the office. Each of our houses told its founder's rise the same way, and no house wrote of another's. On the island, as far as the sermon on Honoratus can be read, the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive: he who had refused to go to the dignity, the dignity came to him. And the one Egyptian bishop Cassian chose to tell us of, Archebius, had been carried off from the anchorites and given to a town as its bishop, and complained that he had been expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of it. Our own teaching made wanting the office a fault. The fathers of Egypt taught that vainglory creates a wish for holy orders, and that the man who wants to rule others has grown cold through pride. So no one in our stories wanted the see. Hear the limit of that. Every one of those stories is a house's own telling of its own founder. Sulpitius was not present at the election, and he was no friend to the bishops who objected. Those bishops left no account; what their case was beyond clothes and hair, no one kept. Whether every reluctance was as whole as our stories say, the men who could have contradicted them never wrote.

quiet.statement: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Even the names you may know for our places are not in our own books, so we do not use them. How do historians know about daily life like ours? From what Cassian said Egypt did, and from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it for a year. From what Sulpitius said the saint did in his cell. Of the island's own day, not a line. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like - only as far as those pages say, and no further.

who_speaks.text: Four figures anchor this world's own voice. Martin was the soldier who left the army for Christ. He was made a bishop against his own will. Sulpitius Severus was the admirer who wrote almost everything we know about him. He admits he was never present for it himself. Cassian lived among Egypt's monks and carried their teaching to Marseilles. He refused to write of wonders. Honoratus founded a community on an island of snakes. Like Martin, he was overtaken by an office he never sought.

documented_stories.teaser: Accused of cowardice for refusing to fight, a soldier offers to walk unarmed toward the enemy line - and the enemy surrenders before morning.
documented_stories.text:
In his Life of St. Martin, Sulpitius Severus records how Martin left the army - the scene the whole of Tours's memory of him turns on.
As barbarian raiders pushed into both divisions of Gaul, Julian Caesar gathered an army at the city of the Vaugiones and began handing a donative to his soldiers, calling them forward one by one. When it came to Martin's turn, he judged it the moment to ask for his discharge: since he did not mean to stay in the service, he did not think it right to take the money. He told Caesar he had served him as a soldier long enough, and now asked to become a soldier to God instead - as the soldier of Christ, he said, it was not lawful for him to fight (his exact words are kept in gallic.quote.martin-refuses-the-donative).
Julian - "the tyrant," in Sulpitius's word - stormed, and accused Martin of withdrawing from fear of the coming battle, not from faith. Martin, only the more resolute for the accusation, answered that if his conduct were taken for cowardice rather than faith, he would stand unarmed before the enemy line the next day, protected by nothing but the sign of the cross (his exact reply is kept in gallic.quote.martin-offers-to-stand-unarmed). He was put back in prison, ready to prove his words true by facing the barbarians unarmed.
On the following day the enemy sent envoys to ask for peace, and surrendered themselves and everything they had. There was no battle. Sulpitius does not leave the reader to draw the conclusion: he asks who can doubt the victory was due to the saintly man, and reads it as the good Lord sparing Martin the sight of others dying - the enemy yielded without bloodshed, and no one was killed.
documented_stories.title: Martin Asks Caesar for His Discharge
documented_stories.when: c. 360, before a battle in Gaul, on the eve of Martin's discharge from the Roman army

floor_note.text: This world confessed what the wider Church confessed about Christ. But its own life rarely argued about it. Vincent, writing from the island, gave one formula as an example of a settled faith, not a live debate: one substance but three Persons in God, two substances but one Person in Christ. He wrote it to defend a different point. Mary should be called the mother of God, he said, not only of the man Christ. A council had already ruled on that, three years before he wrote. This world's real argument lay elsewhere: how much of a monk's own progress comes from God's gift, and how much from his own effort. On that question, this world's own record never reaches a settled answer.

legacy.text: This world's own record stops before its central argument was settled. It says so itself: what comes after is not its to tell. One generation later, the argument about grace and effort continued. But it was no longer monks writing to fellow monks. A bishop trained on the same island took it up instead, writing at the direct request of two church councils. This world's own record ends at the edge of that change, not inside it.

read_first.note: The whole of Martin's own story, told by a man who loved him and was never present for any of it.

relations_summary.text: This world grew up on ground another community had already fought to hold. Before Martin's own household took shape, a bishop named Hilary of Poitiers was sent into exile. He had refused to accept a creed backed by the emperor. Once he came home, Hilary was the bishop near whom Martin first gathered his own followers. This world's own record does not say what happened to Gaul's church after its own span closes in 450. It says nothing about monasticism elsewhere, either.

sourcing.text: This world's record is richest in one man's telling of another. Sulpitius Severus wrote about Martin. Cassian wrote down what Egypt's monks taught him. Both households left rich writing about ideas and virtues. But both leave two things almost entirely dark: the island's own daily life, and Tours's own daily worship. No one wrote down what the brethren sang, or when. No woman's own word survives from either house, though both kept communities of women alongside the men. And a later editor cut three whole sections on the body's own discipline from the one edition of Cassian that survives. That is a gap in what survives, not in what this world itself said.

story.text: This world's own record runs from about 360 to 450 CE, in Roman Gaul. It holds two separate households of monks that never once wrote to each other. One grew up in the Loire valley, around the town of Tours. The other grew up on an island called Lérins, off the Mediterranean coast, and in the nearby city of Marseilles. Nothing in this world's own evidence puts the two households in contact. What holds them together is a shared idea, not a shared conversation. Neither house claims to have invented its own way of life. Both call themselves keepers of what came before them, never authors of something new.

The northern household's founder was a soldier named Martin. Around 360, before a battle, the army was giving out a gift of money to the troops. When his turn came, Martin asked for his discharge instead. He told the commander, named in the record only as Julian Caesar, that he had served him as a soldier long enough; now he would serve Christ, and it was not right for him to fight. Accused of cowardice, Martin offered to walk out unarmed between the two armies the next morning, trusting only the sign of the cross. He never had to. The enemy asked for peace overnight, and the battle never happened. Martin got his discharge and went to Hilary, the bishop of Poitiers.

Years later, the people of Tours wanted Martin as their own bishop. He did not want the office. A citizen named Ruricius lied that his own wife was sick, to draw Martin out of his monastery. Once he was on the road, a crowd blocked every way back, so he could not turn around. A few bishops objected: his clothes were poor and his hair a mess, unfit for so great an honor. The reader picked to read that day's psalm could not get through the crowd. Someone else grabbed the psalter instead and read out whatever verse came open, a line about strength made perfect against enemies. The people cheered, and the objectors fell silent. As bishop, Martin kept living like a monk outside the city walls, and many monks he trained were later made bishops themselves.

Two generations after Martin, a different pattern appeared in the south. A man named Honoratus went alone to a small island off the coast, a place so overrun with snakes that no one else would live there. He went unafraid, singing a psalm, and the record says the snakes gave way before him. He built what his own community later called a camp of God, in a place made for no life at all. Honoratus wanted nothing more than to stay a monk on his island. The office found him anyway: he was made bishop of the nearby city of Arles. Another monk trained on the same island, Faustus, later became bishop of Riez. This world's own record says almost nothing about an ordinary day on the island - only how its founder arrived, and how the office came looking for him.

Both households treated the monks of Egypt as the standard to measure against. But they did it in opposite ways. In the south, the relationship was reception. Cassian's task was to bring the East's customs home to Gaul. He corrected anything built on, in his own words, "the fancy of any one who has founded a monastery." He changed only what the colder climate truly required. In the north, the relationship was comparison, not reception. Sulpitius has a traveler just back from Egypt declare that Martin alone was worth as much as all its hermits and holy men put together. Gaul was a rival to Egypt here, not a debtor. This world's own two households never argued the comparison out with each other. They simply held it in two different ways, at the same time, without ever comparing notes.

Both households also agreed that nothing true could be new. Vincent, a monk on the same island, wrote a short book meant only as a memory aid, "to provide against my forgetfulness," as he put it himself. His test for telling true faith from a corruption dressed up as one was simple: what has been believed everywhere, always, by everyone. He called himself not an author but a keeper, not a teacher but a disciple. Cassian's own writing carried the same conviction north from Egypt. He passed on a story the fathers of Egypt told about themselves: unable to agree how many psalms to sing each evening, they were still arguing when the hour for prayer arrived. One of them rose to sing anyway. He finished the twelfth psalm, said "Alleluia," and vanished. The fathers understood the number to be fixed by that one messenger, not by their own decision. Neither monk chose his own rule. Both received one, and called it received.

The south's own formation program had a name for its goal: purity of heart. Cassian taught that fasting, all-night prayer, and giving up possessions were not the goal itself, only aids toward it. What matters most is discretion, which he called the mother of all virtues - the one that keeps every other virtue from ruining itself through excess. The program named eight faults a monk had to fight in turn, from gluttony to pride, each with its own remedy handed down by the fathers. Tours had no such vocabulary at all. Martin's own record shows a similar instinct at work without ever naming it - his discernment of a false vision of Christ - but it never speaks of purity of heart, discretion, or a fault-list of its own.

The south's most famous argument began, by its own account, as an ordinary worry at prayer. Cassian and his friend Germanus had spent an evening in Egypt listening to an elder teach on chastity. The elder ended with one troubling sentence: that no one becomes master of the good by his own effort alone. The next morning, still turning it over, they asked him to explain himself. He answered with a farmer's field. A farmer who will not plow gets no harvest - his effort matters. But even a hard-working farmer gets nothing without rain he cannot make happen himself. The elder concluded that the very wish to do good starts with God, and it is for us to follow that grace day by day. That morning's answer grew into a whole argument about how much of a monk's progress is God's gift and how much is his own labor - an argument that later reached Rome, and this world's own record never settles it.

At Tours, the record is organized around a different idea entirely: power, felt and shown. Martin once found a catechumen, a new believer not yet baptized, lying dead. He shut himself alone with the body, stretched himself over it, and after two hours the man opened his eyes. Another night, the devil came to Martin dressed as Christ, in royal purple and a jeweled crown. Martin refused to believe him: the only Christ he would accept still carried the marks of his own wounds. Cassian, in the south, refused this whole way of measuring a monk. He would not, in his own words, weave a tale of God's wonders and signs, and warned that a monk who boasts of casting out demons has already failed. The two households never argued this difference out either. One built its record around power. The other built its record around refusing to.

Bishops and church councils sat at the center of this world's deepest disagreement with itself. At Tours, the office was something to be wary of: bishops resisted Martin's election, and some of his own accusers turned out to be bishops themselves. The emperor once called Martin to court, to stop tribunes being sent to hunt heretics in Spain. Martin agreed to share communion there with bishops he had refused before - the same bishops who had pushed for a heretic's execution. He did it to save lives, then regretted it for the rest of his own life. He never sat with a group of bishops again. His discipline reached his own household, too, and not always gently. A presbyter he had raised from boyhood was named Brictio. People inside Martin's own community accused Brictio of buying enslaved children - boys taken from beyond the frontier, and girls chosen, the record says, for their looks. When Martin corrected him, Brictio raged at his own master in public, calling his visions ridiculous fancies. He repented within the hour. Martin never removed him from office, saying: "If Christ bore with Judas, why should not I bear with Brictio?" In the south, by contrast, church councils were trusted as guardians of the truth, not as something to flee. This world's own record does not resolve the disagreement between its two households. It states it plainly and leaves it standing.

Almost everything this world's northern half knows comes from one writer. Sulpitius Severus was a wealthy layman who gave up his own career to follow Martin. He was never present for any of the events he describes, and he says so himself. His real sources were Martin's own household, and sometimes Martin himself. That single-author risk runs through every surviving Tours story. When Martin's own death drew near, he traveled to make peace among quarreling clergy in a nearby town. He already knew he was dying. His own monks wanted to lay him on a soft bed of straw. He refused. He chose sackcloth and ashes instead, saying he had sinned if he left his monks a different example to follow. He was carried back to Tours. A crowd the record puts at two thousand buried him: monks, old men, young soldiers who had just sworn service to Christ, and a choir of consecrated women who held back their own tears out of modesty.

dates.display: d. 397, on a peacemaking journey to Condate; a soldier under 'Julian Caesar' in his youth, discharged at a donative; monk 'not far from the town' where Hilary was bishop, then bishop of Tours from an undated election (the monastery across the river founded 'after 371' only on the editorial introduction's word); 'lived sixteen years' after the Treves affair by Gallus's own reckoning

voices.hedge: Everything told about Martin comes from one writer, Sulpitius Severus, who loved him and was never present for any of it. Sulpitius says so himself. That single-author risk runs through every story this world tells about its own founder.
voices.text: Martin left the army to serve Christ instead, telling his commander it was not right for him to fight. He gathered followers in the woods near Tours, then was made bishop against his own will. As bishop, he never stopped living like a monk. He healed the sick and raised the dead, by his own account, yet felt that power lessen once he took a communion he believed was wrong, just to save two men's lives. He never sat with a group of bishops again.

dates.display: travelled in Egypt with Germanus in his youth (the interval to his writing not stated in this world's own documents); founded the twin houses at Marseilles c. 415; wrote the Institutes for Castor before 426 and the Conferences in three parts, Part II (to Honoratus and Eucherius) not later than 426; d. c. 435

names.name: Cassian, the founder of the houses at Marseilles

voices.hedge: Cassian never mentions Martin, and no surviving story shows a Gallic monk actually keeping the Egyptian program he wrote down. By his own complaint, no one in his own monasteries kept it even for a year.
voices.text: Cassian lived for years among the monks of Egypt before founding two communities of his own at Marseilles. He wrote down what he had learned there, refusing on principle to tell any tale of wonders or signs. He passed on Egypt's own program: purity of heart as the goal, discretion as the guide, and eight faults for a monk to fight in order. He also passed on an unresolved question, one he did not shy from: how much of a monk's progress is God's own gift, and how much is his own effort.

dates.display: founded the community on the island of Lerins c. 400-410 (410 on the surviving volume's editorial introduction); addressed by Cassian as a brother presiding over a large monastery, then as a bishop - the see identified as Arles, from 426, only by the editorial apparatus; d. c. 429/430, the year his disciple and successor Hilary preached his life

names.name: Honoratus, the founder of the island
Honoratus of Lerins, later bishop of Arles (d. c. 429/430)

voices.hedge: The only story told of Honoratus comes from a funeral sermon preached by his own disciple, read today only in rough, hard-to-read Latin. What survives can tell how he arrived on the island and how he left it - nothing of what happened in between.
voices.text: Honoratus went alone to an island so overrun with snakes that no one else would live there, and built a community in a place made for no life at all. He wanted nothing more than to stay a monk. The office of bishop found him anyway, and he ended his life leading the church at Arles instead of the island he founded.

dates.display: writing c. 397 (the Life; Letter III within months of Martin's death) to c. 404-406 (the Dialogues); an Aquitanian 'of an illustrious family' who visited Martin at Tours; birth and death years rest only on the modern editors' disagreeing endnotes and are not asserted

voices.hedge: Nearly everything this world knows about its own northern half passes through this one author's hand. He was not a neutral reporter - he loved Martin and wrote to make readers admire him. Every surviving claim about Tours carries that single-author risk.
voices.text: Sulpitius Severus was rich and well-educated. He gave up his own career to follow Martin. He wrote Martin's Life while Martin was still alive. He says plainly that he was never there for any of the events in it. His real sources were Martin's own household, and sometimes Martin himself.

tile.text: Between about 360 and 450 CE, two households in Roman Gaul lived out one shared idea in different ways: a monk does not stop being a monk just because the Church makes him a bishop. In the Loire valley, a soldier named Martin left the army to serve Christ instead. He gathered followers in the woods near Tours, and the townspeople later seized him and made him their bishop. He never gave up his monk's life. Two generations later, on an island called Lérins off the Mediterranean coast, and in the nearby city of Marseilles, other monks built communities of their own. One of them, John Cassian, had lived among the monks of Egypt. He wrote down what he learned there and adapted it for a colder land and a different church. Another, Vincent, wrote a short rule for telling true growth in the faith from a corruption dressed up as one. Running through both households was one argument, never fully settled: how much of a monk's progress is God's own gift, and how much is his own effort. The two households never had any contact with each other that the surviving evidence can show. The story closes around 450, before that argument hardened into fixed camps.
